Module 3 · Lesson 4

Simulation, Virtual Reality & Transfer

When real-world practice is difficult, expensive, or risky, can a simulation build a skill that actually transfers?

~25–30 min Builds on transfer & specificity Closes Week 3
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to…

  • 1Distinguish simulators from virtual reality as practice environments.
  • 2Explain how transfer, time, cost, availability, and safety affect whether simulation is worthwhile.
  • 3Distinguish physical fidelity from psychological fidelity and explain why both matter.
  • 4Interpret evidence from a clinical VR training study and connect it to specificity of practice.
The question that follows from specificity

If learning is specific to what we practice, then a simulation is useful only to the extent that what is learned there carries into the real task.

That makes simulation and VR a direct application of the ideas from the previous lessons:

  • →Transfer: does practice in one environment improve performance somewhere else?
  • →Specificity: how closely does the practice environment reproduce the demands of the target task?

Evaluating simulator effectiveness

The simulator has to earn its place

A sophisticated training environment is not automatically an effective one. The key question is whether the transfer produced by the training justifies the resources spent on it.

Effectiveness

How much transfer?

Does practice in the simulator produce better performance on the target task than the learner would otherwise show?

Efficiency

How much transfer per unit of training?

Does the simulator save time or make training more practical when its cost, availability, and safety are considered?

The decision is practical as well as scientific

A simulator can produce positive transfer and still be a poor choice if it requires too much time or cost relative to the benefit. Conversely, even modest transfer may be valuable if real practice is dangerous or unavailable.

Simulator fidelity

What exactly needs to be “realistic”?

Fidelity is not one thing. Two complementary forms matter:

Physical fidelity

How similar are the task features?

The degree to which features of the simulation and the transfer task themselves are identical.

Psychological fidelity

How similar are the required behaviors and processes?

The degree to which the behaviors and processes produced in the simulator replicate those required by the transfer task.

Complementary, not competing

High physical fidelity does not automatically guarantee high psychological fidelity, and the reverse can also be true.

Apply the distinction

Which kind of fidelity is being emphasized?

Select each scenario to reveal the interpretation.

VR fidelity

VR has strengths — and a common limitation

VR can provide repeated practice of perceptual, decision-making, and movement demands that are difficult to reproduce otherwise. But VR often lacks some of the inherent feedback from hands-on tools that a physical simulator can provide.

General principle

VR training should transfer best when it provides sufficient physical and psychological fidelity for the aspects of the target task that matter.

Clinical transfer study

Does immersive VR improve surgical performance?

Here is an example of a research study in this domain. McKinney et al. (2022) asked whether practice in an immersive VR environment would transfer to better performance on a realistic surgical task. They compared VR training with traditional technique-guide preparation for partial knee replacement.

Study design

  • 22 orthopedic surgery residents (PGY-1 to PGY-5)
  • Randomized to VR training or a traditional technique guide
  • Transfer task: perform the procedure on a SawBones model using standard surgical trays
  • Performance rated by a blinded observer

McKinney et al. (2022). Virtual Reality Training in Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty: A Randomized, Blinded Trial. Journal of Surgical Education, 79(6), 1526–1535.

The result

The VR training transferred

On the realistic surgical transfer task, the VR-trained residents showed several advantages over the technique-guide group.

✓

More steps completed correctly

The VR group performed more of the procedure correctly.

26.7

Faster completion

26.7 minutes for VR versus 35.4 minutes for the technique-guide group.

4/5

Higher global ratings

The VR group scored higher in four of five global assessment categories.

↓

Less study time

The VR group reached the same or better proficiency with shorter study time.

Take-home message

Immersive VR produced better transfer to a realistic surgical simulation than traditional study in this experiment. The result fits the specificity of practice principle: the VR condition gave learners practice that more closely resembled the target performance demands.

Knowledge check

Which feature of the McKinney study makes it a test of transfer, rather than merely a comparison of performance inside the VR system?

Week 3 wrap-up

What you can now do

  • 1Explain why simulation is fundamentally a transfer problem.
  • 2Distinguish a physical simulator from virtual reality and explain when each may be useful.
  • 3Evaluate simulation using transfer, time, cost, availability, safety, and possible time savings.
  • 4Distinguish physical fidelity from psychological fidelity.
  • 5Use the McKinney surgical-training study as an example of positive transfer from immersive VR.
The through-line for the week

Individual learners differ. Practice quality matters. Learning is specific. Transfer depends on shared demands. Simulation and VR are useful when they reproduce enough of those demands to make practice carry into the real task.
